{{Short description|Algebraic structure}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''p''-stable group}}
In [[finite group theory]], a '''''p''-stable group''' for an [[odd prime]] ''p'' is a [[finite group]] satisfying a technical condition introduced by {{harvs|txt|last=Gorenstein|last2=Walter|year1=1964|loc1=p.169|year2=1965}} in order to extend Thompson's uniqueness results in the [[odd order theorem]] to groups with dihedral Sylow 2-subgroups.

== Definitions ==

There are several equivalent definitions of a ''p''-stable group.

=== Glauberman ===

We give definition of a ''p''-stable group in two parts.  The definition used here comes from {{harv|Glauberman|1968|p=1104}}.

'''1'''. Let ''p'' be an odd prime and ''G'' be a finite group with a nontrivial ''p''-core <math>O_p(G)</math>.  Then ''G'' is ''p''-stable if it satisfies the following condition:  Let ''P'' be an arbitrary ''p''-subgroup of ''G'' such that <math>O_{p'\!}(G)</math> is a [[normal subgroup]] of ''G''.  Suppose that <math>x \in N_G(P)</math> and <math>\bar x</math> is the [[coset]] of <math>C_G(P)</math> containing ''x''. If <math>[P,x,x]=1</math>, then <math>\overline{x}\in O_n(N_G(P)/C_G(P))</math>.

Now, define <math>\mathcal{M}_p(G)</math> as the [[set (mathematics)|set]] of all ''p''-subgroups of ''G'' maximal with respect to the property that <math>O_p(M)\not= 1</math>.

'''2'''. Let ''G'' be a finite group and ''p'' an odd prime.  Then ''G'' is called ''p''-stable if every element of <math>\mathcal{M}_p(G)</math> is ''p''-stable by definition '''1'''.

=== Alternative ===

Let ''p'' be an odd prime and ''H'' a finite group.  Then ''H'' is ''p''-stable if <math>F^*(H)=O_p(H)</math> and, whenever ''P'' is a normal ''p''-subgroup of ''H'' and <math>g \in H</math> with <math>[P,g,g]=1</math>, then <math>gC_H(P)\in O_p(H/C_H(P))</math>.

== Properties ==

If ''p'' is an odd prime and ''G'' is a finite group such that SL<sub>2</sub>(''p'') is not involved in ''G'', then ''G'' is ''p''-stable.  If furthermore ''G'' contains a normal ''p''-subgroup ''P'' such that <math>C_G(P)\leqslant P</math>, then <math>Z(J_0(S))</math> is a [[characteristic subgroup]] of ''G'', where <math>J_0(S)</math> is the subgroup introduced by [[John G. Thompson|John Thompson]] in {{harv|Thompson|1969|pp=149–151}}.
